RETR recorded transfers · Jan 2 to Aug 31, 2026 · 72 counties

Wisconsin Housing Market 2026: Findings for Investors

What the six pages of the Lumen report show, how far each finding can be trusted, and where the dashboard needs a second look.

SummaryHow to read thisMarket pulsePricesCountiesBuyersIncome and landDistressBy strategyLimitsDefinitions

The short version

Through August 2026, Wisconsin's market shows rising prices at every level, a June sales peak, and a buyer pool that uses a mortgage less often each month. Foreclosures are small next to sales and concentrated in Milwaukee. The file covers a single year, so it cannot separate a lasting rise from the normal spring and summer lift. Read the price gain as a seasonal-window measurement until it can be compared with 2025.

Two places the dashboard can mislead

Its county ranking uses average prices, and a few expensive sales can lift a small county's average. Green Lake tops the list at +44.3%, while its median rose 5.5%. Second, a coding change in January makes that month's estate and foreclosure counts too low. Both are covered below, and neither changes the report's arithmetic, which was recomputed independently and matched.

How to read this report

The source is tranferData.csv, Wisconsin's Real Estate Transfer Return (RETR) filings for January through August 2026. Every deed recorded with a transfer return appears there, including gifts, trusts and corrections. The Lumen report narrows those to arm's-length sales: full-parcel, full-ownership sales of at least $10,000 between unrelated parties. All prices and shares here use those sales unless stated otherwise.

Most comparisons use two windows: January to April against May to August. Because the second window always holds the warmer months, a statewide change mixes real appreciation with season. County results are shown relative to the state ("vs WI"), which removes the shared seasonal lift. Those differences are in percentage points.

Each section names the Lumen page it explains and shows that page as it renders. Confidence labels are my judgment of how well a finding survives the checks described in each section. Tables and charts marked as additions go beyond the Lumen report, because Lumen's query language has no median or percentile function.

Lumen page 1: Market Pulse

Activity peaked in June, and three counties hold a third of the money

Monthly sales climbed from a February low of 5,760 to 11,587 in June, then eased to 10,375 in August. That is the shape a Wisconsin buyer would expect from the season, but with one year of data the size of the lift cannot be judged against a normal year. Single-family sales were 62.5% higher in May to August than in January to April.

Single-family homes are 66% of dollar volume, followed by commercial at 14%. Dane ($3.64B), Milwaukee ($3.33B) and Waukesha ($2.80B) together account for 33.2% of all dollars, so statewide averages lean heavily on southeastern and Madison-area pricing.

Lumen page 2: Price Trends

Prices rose from the bottom of the market to the top

The average single-family price moved from $361,285 in January to April to $394,117 in May to August, a gain of 9.1%. The median, which ignores the size of the very largest sales, rose 9.7%. When two measures of the middle agree this closely, a handful of expensive homes is not driving the result.

Three further checks point the same way:

  • Whole distribution. From January to August the 25th percentile rose from $200,000 to $225,000 and the 90th from $605,000 to $682,000.
  • County mix. Holding each county's share of sales fixed gives +8.7%, so a shift toward pricier counties explains only about 0.4 points of the 9.1%. Milwaukee's share of sales did fall, from 13.9% to 12.5%.
  • Dropping January. February to April against May to August gives +8.7% on the average and +9.0% on the median.

What this cannot rule out is a shift in the kind of home selling. Larger homes may simply list in summer. Square footage is too sparsely filled in the file to adjust for it.

The band mix shows the same move. Sales under $150,000 fell from 13.6% to 11.1% of single-family sales between the windows, and sales at $500,000 and above rose from 18.9% to 23.0%. The largest gain in share came at $500,000 to $1 million.

Lumen page 3: Where to Look

County rankings are a watchlist, and a short one

This page ranks counties by how much faster their average price rose than the state's, using single-family sales in counties with at least 30 sales in each window. It is the page most likely to be over-read, so I tested it two ways: whether the median agrees with the average, and how much the result moves when the county's sales are resampled.

The chart below shows the ten strongest and ten weakest counties. The bar is a 90% interval from 2,000 resamples. A filled dot means the whole interval sits on one side of zero. Of 70 counties, 6 clear that bar upward and 5 downward. With a 90% interval, about 7 of 70 would clear it by chance if no county truly differed from the state, so the real count of outliers is small.

Why Green Lake is not the top county

Green Lake's average rose from $335,009 to $483,367, the largest gain in the state. Its median went from $237,000 to $250,000. Five of the county's six highest sales came in the later window, and five of the six were in the Town of Green Lake. Those sales lifted the average, and the typical home barely moved. Bayfield and Burnett also fail the interval test.

The better-supported counties

Counties clearing the interval test, single-family sales (addition to the Lumen report)
CountySalesAvg priceAvg changeMedian changeVs WINote

Racine is the most credible strong county, because 1,696 sales leave little room for noise and its median (+16.1%) backs its average (+19.5%). Its sales grew more slowly than the state's, so higher prices came with relatively fewer transactions. Sheboygan and Eau Claire are similar, with enough sales to take seriously and prices below the state average. Polk and Oconto are smaller, with more non-owner buying than the state (32.7% and 45.8%, against 28.3%). Langlade barely clears the test and also has the state's highest foreclosure rate, so separate distressed sales from regular ones before reading its gain as appreciation.

On the weak side, Winnebago and St. Croix matter most because they are large enough to be real. St. Croix's median rose only 0.8%, and Winnebago's 4.4%, against 9.7% statewide. Crawford, Price and Taylor are small rural counties where a few sales can shift the result.

The biggest markets match the state. Dane (+8.2%, median +5.3%), Milwaukee (+10.5%, median +11.5%) and Waukesha (+11.3%, median +6.1%) all have intervals that cross zero, so none differs clearly from the state. Dane is notable for its low non-owner share of 15.9%, against 34.5% in Milwaukee.

Lumen page 4: Who Is Buying

More buyers are paying without a mortgage

This is the strongest trend in the file. The share of sales recorded with no financing rose from 35.2% in January to 43.7% in August. The pattern holds within single-family (30.8% to 36.5% between the windows) and among individual buyers of single-family homes, where it rose every month, from 20.0% to 33.9%. The field is filled on every arm's-length sale, so missing answers do not explain it.

Two cautions apply. "No financing" means no financing was reported on the return, which is a proxy for cash. Equity lines or private loans would not show as a mortgage. And the data has no mortgage rates, ages or incomes, so it shows that cash buying increased but not why. Summer second-home purchases are one candidate, since no-financing sales skew cheaper (median $252,000 against $328,000 with financing) and are common in land and vacation segments.

Investors did not retreat

The dashboard's falling entity share can look like investors leaving. The counts say otherwise. Purchases by LLCs, partnerships and corporations rose from 1,470 in January to a June peak of 1,721, and were 1,590 in August. Individual buyers rose much faster, from 4,546 to 8,174, which pushed the entity share down. In single-family alone, entity purchases went from 515 to 791 a month. Non-owner share behaves the same way, falling from 38.2% to 28.4% in July and turning up to 30.6% in August.

Out-of-state buyers are vacation-market buyers

Out-of-state buyers made 4,855 purchases, 7.1% of sales with a known state, and that share stayed between 6.6% and 8.0% all year. They pay about twice as much (average $766,997, against $391,438 for others), and 63.6% use no financing. Of those who answered the residence question, 91.3% will not live in the property. Half of their purchases are single-family homes, and another fifth are vacant land.

Geography follows the state line. Illinois buyers go to Walworth (291), Kenosha (113) and Milwaukee (107), then north to Vilas and Adams. Minnesota buyers go to Burnett (175), Polk (145), St. Croix (129) and Douglas (91). State is read from the buyer's mailing address, so a buyer who has already moved to Wisconsin counts as in-state.

Lumen page 5: Income Property & Land

Small multi-family is the deep market, and prices per door show no trend

Multi-family counts split sharply by size. Duplexes through fourplexes are 2,015 of 2,296 deals with a unit count, while 79 properties of 20 or more units account for almost the same dollars. Price per door is close across sizes, and small buildings carry the highest figure.

The statewide price per door of $127,635 moves between about $104,000 and $139,000 with no direction. February's $192,070 comes from two Kenosha County deals, $64.0M for 54 units and $36.0M for 76, so it is not a market move. Milwaukee has the most activity (940 sales at $104,344 a door). Dane is $119,827 on 164 sales and Brown is $108,038. Kenosha's $300,082 reflects those same large deals on only 48 sales. The file has no rents, so these figures cannot produce a cap rate.

Commercial

There were 3,207 commercial and industrial sales worth $4.24B, and entities made 81.5% of those purchases. The median deal is $465,003 against an average of $1.32M. The ten largest deals are 11.3% of dollars, so the market is broader than the headline deals suggest. Three of the five largest are in Kenosha and Racine counties: $87.0M for a Pleasant Prairie manufacturing property, $71.4M in Caledonia and $47.5M in Pleasant Prairie. Mequon ($62.5M) and Glendale ($45.4M) complete the five.

Land

Land is mostly lots. The median parcel is 1.2 acres and 75.9% of sales have no financing. Two per-acre figures tell different stories, and both are correct. Weighting by acres gives $23,548, because large rural tracts dominate the total. The median parcel sold for $51,450 an acre. Dane ($187,710) and Milwaukee ($259,212) are lot prices, not raw acreage values. Farm and forest parcels are larger (median 29.4 acres) and sold at $14,821 an acre.

Lumen page 6: Distress & Supply

Foreclosures are low and concentrated, and January's count is understated

There were 759 foreclosure transfers, about 10.7 for every 1,000 arm's-length sales. The count held near 100 a month from February through July. August's 71 is the lowest since January, but recent filings can lag, so one low month is not a trend. Bank and agency resales are only 128 statewide, too few to support a distressed-inventory strategy on their own.

The January coding change

Conveyance codes changed partway through January. Before about January 12 almost nothing was coded "Termination of decedent's interest" or "Trust (conveyance to)", and those transfers landed in "Other", which ran at 3,088 for the month against about 800 afterward. So the rise in estate transfers from 1,129 in January to 2,047 in February is a coding effect, and January's 48 foreclosures probably is too. Arm's-length sales are much less exposed, since the "Sale" code was in use throughout. Only 46 January "Other" transfers looked like unrelated sales of $10,000 or more.

Milwaukee is the only county where the count and the rate are both high: it has 30.4% of the state's foreclosures, more than seven times Racine's 30. The rural rates above rest on small counts. Timeshares are excluded, because 74 foreclosure transfers at timeshare parcels, mostly in Walworth County, would otherwise overstate distress there.

Future supply

Estate transfers total 17,090, running about 2,100 to 2,500 a month after January. These are ownership changes at death and trustee distributions, so not all of these properties will sell, but some will become listings. Estates are already 2.7% of arm's-length sellers. Land contracts are a thin 1.3% of sales.

What this suggests by strategy

These are starting points for further work. The data shows recorded prices and buyers, with no rents, listings, or condition.

Limits of the data

  • One year only. No year-over-year figure is possible, and season cannot be measured. This is the main limit on every statewide trend. Adding the 2025 RETR files would fix it, and Lumen's Refresh would pick them up with little rework.
  • Prices are not quality-adjusted. The same house is not being compared over time. A repeat-sales measure would need more than eight months.
  • Averages are outlier-sensitive. Lumen shows averages because it has no median. Small-county figures should be checked against the table in this report.
  • Recording lag. Dates are recording dates. The latest months may gain late filings, especially foreclosures.
  • Proxies. No financing, mailing-address state and the residence answer are all self-reported or inferred. The residence question is blank on 13% to 19% of sales each month, so that share uses answered returns only.
  • Parsing. Ten malformed CSV rows, from about five transfers with stray quotes in their legal descriptions, have no sale price and are excluded. Five transfers cannot move any figure here noticeably.

How the figures were checked

Every Lumen figure used here was recomputed separately in Python from the same CSV and matched exactly, including 70,681 sales and the $417,234 average. Medians, percentiles, intervals, deal-size tables and the coding-change analysis are additions from that same recomputation. The Lumen report itself also passed live checks: slicing to Dane returned $566,135 and 6,009 sales, and refreshing from the CSV kept 147,382 rows.

Definitions

Arm's-length saleConveyance is Sale, parties unrelated, entire parcel, full ownership, price at least $10,000, not a WDOT document, not a timeshare.
SegmentsCondo, Multi-family, Commercial (Class 2, manufacturing, utility, telephone), Farm & forest (Class 4, 5m, 6), Land, Single family (Class 1), Other. Timeshares are separated.
Price Change 4MAverage price in the latest four months against the prior four.
Vs WICounty change minus state change, in percentage points. Needs 30 or more sales in each window.
90% intervalSales in each window are resampled 2,000 times. The range holds the middle 90% of the resulting vs WI values. The state figure is held fixed.
Entity buyerLLC, partnership, corporation, REIT or financial institution. Trusts are counted separately.
Non-owner shareBuyers answering No to the primary residence question, out of those answering.
Out of stateBuyer mailing address outside Wisconsin, out of 68,377 sales with a readable state.
Price per doorTotal multi-family dollars divided by total units, for buildings of two or more units.
Price per acreTotal dollars divided by total acres, for parcels of 0 to 10,000 acres. The median is computed per parcel.
ForeclosuresAll foreclosure, judgment and county foreclosure transfers, excluding timeshares. Counted among all transfers, not only sales.
Estate transfersTermination of decedent's interest, will or survivorship, PR-1831 affidavit, and trustee to beneficiary.
Prepared November 1, 2026 from Wisconsin Housing Market 2026.lumen and tranferData.csv.
